title: OAuth 2.0 Roles and Flows
description: Learn the four OAuth 2.0 roles — resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server — and when to use each of the main authorization flows. Apply this knowledge in .NET backends and JavaScript frontends.

data.text: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that lets applications obtain limited access to user accounts on an HTTP service. Instead of sharing the user's password, the application receives an access token that represents delegated permission. OAuth 2.0 defines four roles and several grant types (flows) that fit different application types, from web apps to server-to-server APIs.

data.title: Core roles
items: **Resource Owner**: The person or system that owns the protected data. Usually a human user who can grant access.
**Client**: The application requesting access to the resource owner's data. This could be a web app, mobile app, or backend service.
**Authorization Server**: The server that authenticates the resource owner and issues access tokens after getting consent.
**Resource Server**: The API that hosts the protected data. It validates access tokens and serves the requested resources.

terms.definition: The entity capable of granting access to a protected resource, typically the end user.
The application requesting access on behalf of the resource owner.
A credential used to access protected resources. Typically expires in minutes or hours.
The method an OAuth client uses to request an access token.

data.title: OAuth authorization code flow overview
data.content: The client redirects the user to the authorization server, the user consents, and the server redirects back with a code that the client exchanges for tokens.
data.code:
1. GET https://auth.example.com/authorize
   ?response_type=code
   &client_id=my-app-id
   &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback
   &scope=openid profile email
   &state=random-123

2. User authenticates and consents

3. Redirect to https://app.example.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=random-123

4. POST https://auth.example.com/oauth/token
   grant_type=authorization_code
   &code=AUTH_CODE
   &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback
   &client_id=my-app-id
   &client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET

5. Response: { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in }

data.text: The **authorization code flow** is the most secure and widely used flow. The client never sees the user's password. Instead, the authorization server issues a short-lived authorization code that the client exchanges for tokens through a back-channel POST request. Because the client secret is included in the token exchange, only the real application can complete the flow.
Other Flows and When to Use Them

The **implicit flow** was designed for browser-based SPAs but is now discouraged because tokens are returned directly in the URL fragment, exposing them to browser history and referrer leaks. The **resource owner password credentials flow** sends the user's username and password directly to the client — this should only be used for highly trusted first-party apps. The **client credentials flow** is for machine-to-machine communication where no user is involved.

cards.title: Authorization Code
cards.description: The standard flow for web apps and SPAs with a backend. Most secure option for user-facing apps.
pros: Tokens never touch the browser URL
cons: Requires a backend to exchange the code

cards.title: Implicit
cards.description: Deprecated flow that returned tokens directly in the URL fragment.

cards.title: Resource Owner Password
cards.description: The app collects the user's password and exchanges it for tokens. Only for first-party highly trusted apps.
cons: Phishing risk if app is compromised
Cannot enforce MFA at the authorization server

cards.title: Client Credentials
cards.description: Machine-to-machine flow. The client authenticates with its own credentials and receives a token.

data.text: ASP.NET Core has built-in OpenID Connect middleware that handles the authorization code flow automatically. You configure the authority, client ID, and scopes, and the middleware manages redirects, token storage, and user authentication. For machine-to-machine flows, use the client credentials flow with Microsoft.Identity.Web or a custom token-acquisition service.

data.title: OpenID Connect in ASP.NET Core
data.content: Configure the OpenID Connect handler to use the authorization code flow.

items.text: Use the authorization code flow with PKCE for all browser-based apps.
items.hint: PKCE removes the need for a client secret in public clients.

items.text: Never use the implicit flow for new applications.
items.hint: It is deprecated in the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP and exposes tokens in URLs.

items.text: Use client credentials only for machine-to-machine APIs.
items.hint: It does not represent a user and cannot be used for user-specific authorization.

items.text: Always use the state parameter in authorization requests.
items.hint: The state parameter prevents CSRF attacks on the authorization flow.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: OAuth 2.0 defines four roles: resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server.
The authorization code flow is the safest choice for user-facing web and mobile apps.
The implicit flow is deprecated; use authorization code with PKCE instead.
Client credentials are for machine-to-machine communication, not user impersonation.
data.takeaway: Choose the flow that matches your client type, and always prefer the authorization code flow with PKCE for browsers.
